title: Alert Rules: Threshold-Based Monitoring
content:
Alert rules define conditions on intelligence metrics that trigger when checked against live data. Each rule specifies a domain, metric, comparison operator, and threshold value.

Anatomy of a rule: A rule has a unique id, a domain (markets, conflicts, cyber, weather, military, health), a metric name within that domain (e.g., spy_price, event_count), an operator (gt, lt, gte, lte, eq, ne, contains), a threshold value, and a human-readable message describing what the alert means.

Operators: gt (greater than), lt (less than), gte (greater than or equal), lte (less than or equal), eq (equals), ne (not equals), contains (string/array containment check).

Evaluation: When alert_check() runs, it fetches current data for each rule's domain, extracts the specified metric, applies the operator against the threshold, and reports whether the rule is triggered. Results include the current value, whether the rule fired, and the rule's message.

Sentinel integration: The sentinel scheduler periodically evaluates all alert rules as part of its autonomous monitoring cycle. Triggered alerts are included in sentinel reports and can be forwarded to cb-control for iOS push notifications.

Storage: Rules persist as JSON in the alerts/ subdirectory of the MCP data directory. They survive restarts and are shared across sessions.

Best practices: Use descriptive rule IDs and messages. Set thresholds based on domain knowledge — anomaly_scan() can help identify normal baselines. Start with a few high-confidence rules and refine over time. Use alert_check({ rule_id: "id" }) to test individual rules before relying on them in production.
